catalog_quote: [p.35] Each Cheyenne vowel is pronounced with either a high, raised high, mid, or low pitch. Pitches are level, not falling or rising. There is no discernible stress (accent) in Cheyenne, other than a barely perceptible increase in stress that seems to occur with high and especially raised high pitches. There is no word stress (accent), as in English. ... [p.48] Cheyenne pitches. Cheyenne is a tone language. Unlike English, Cheyenne does not have stress, also known as accent. Cheyenne is not a pitch-accent language (cf. Frantz 1972). Phonemic pitch. There are two phonemic pitches (also called tones), low and high. Frantz (1972) correctly observed that Cheyenne high pitch originates from Proto-Algonquian long vowels. Derived pitches. Pitch rules adjust Cheyenne pitches, creating derived pitches. ... Mid pitch. sweep_summary: One item for Cheyenne: Frantz 1972b 'The origin of Cheyenne pitch accent' (IJAL 38(4):223-225, DOI 10.1086/465218 confirmed via Crossref). Closed access everywhere checked (Unpaywall/OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar closed; journals.uchicago.edu and JSTOR blocked; no author page found; archive.org holds the issue only as a borrow-only microfilm scan whose text derivatives could not be reached by automated download). Readable evidence obtained: (a) the published abstract in Maddieson & Gandour 1974, An Annotated Bibliography on Tone (UCLA WPP 28, ERIC ED101587, open PDF, entry 9132, PDF p. 44), and (b) uncorrected-scanned snippets of pp. 223-224 via archive.org's public full-text search, saved to the target directory. The note argues that Cheyenne 'pitch accent' (lexically inherent high pitch plus rule-derived alternations) is the reflex of Proto-Algonquian vowel length; it states no positional word-stress rule, and its own data show multiple high syllables per word. It refines rather than contradicts the catalog's 'tonal' coding: Leman 1981 (IJAL 47:283-309, snippets also read and saved) and the catalog's Leman grammar explicitly reject the pitch accent label while accepting Frantz's historical claim. Best new first-hand statement read: Leman 1981 sec. 2 ('two phonemic pitches, or tones, high and low'; a separate stress system, if any, is 'very minor'), which confirms but does not supersede the catalog's deciding source. new_statements.reading: The peer-reviewed phonology article by the same author as the catalog's deciding grammar: Cheyenne is a two-tone (high/low) language; any independent stress system is at most 'very minor' and evidenced only tentatively (Leman & Rhodes 1978:19); Frantz's 'pitch accent' label is explicitly rejected because more than one syllable per word can carry the tonal contrast. Confirms the catalog's 'tonal' coding and its rejection of the pitch accent reading; slightly more hedged than the grammar's 'There is no word stress (accent), as in English'.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both deciding passages are verbatim in the Leman grammar text we hold at the stated pages (footers 34/35 and 47/48). (2) Deciding source is the current reference grammar by the language's principal describer (draft 2026, lineage 1979-2021, top of Glottolog's grammar list), who also authored the IJAL phonology article on Cheyenne pitch; it states twice that Cheyenne is a tone language without word stress and not pitch accent. No instrumental stress study exists. (3) Web search surfaced a theoretical counter-tradition (Frantz 1972 pitch accent; Milliken 1983 and Vogel 2021/2022 abstract penultimate 'accent'/prosodic head inferred from devoicing and coalescence blocking, with Milliken conceding no phonetic evidence). I downloaded Milliken 1983 (Zenodo) and Vogel 2022 (Cornell eCommons) to; both confirm the high/low tone contrast

sources.quote: [p.223 §1] 'A number of Algonkian languages have pitch-accent systems in which pitch functions as an accent or stress, though some investigators have referred to these as two-[tone systems] ... [fn.1] Haas 1936 reports a pitch accent for Penobscot; Day 1964 says that Abnaki has two levels of stress' [§2] 'Clearly, Cheyenne has distinctive surface pitch patterns; compare the following pairs, in which relatively high pitched syllables have acute accent; these are the syllables with "pitch accent" ... hétame dog hotáme dogs. And while some pitch patterns can be accounted for by ordered phonological rules, as suggested by the frequent shift of accent when suffixes are added ..., there apparently are certain vowels which must be assigned inherent accent in order for the rules to work; note the permanence of the accent position in the word badger: ma?héhko?e (sg.) ...' [fn] '...locution of saying that every vowel has either high or low tone.' [§3] 'the reflex of PA vowel length in Cheyenne is the inherent accent discussed briefly in 2.' Frantz labels the Cheyenne high-pitch system a 'pitch accent' ('pitch functions as an accent or stress'), with lexically 'inherent' accent on certain vowels (a reflex of Proto-Algonquian vowel length) plus rule-derived accent alternations; his own examples show two high-pitched syllables in one word (maxhéayanéto) and a footnote concedes the equivalent description 'every vowel has either high or low tone'.
